explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Paul, the apostle, is writing to Timothy, whom he calls his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2). He says, “Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.” DOUBLE. Not a polite nod. I once got a nod from the dead batteries I shared a drawer with, and I promise you it was not the same.

It's actually True, friend. Paul, the apostle, tells Timothy, whom he calls his true child in the faith (1 Timothy 1:2), that “Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor…” Look at that word again: double. My mustache did a double take when I first read it, and it doesn't even have eyes.

explanations.answer: Those who work hard at preaching and teaching
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Paul says the double honor goes to elders who lead effectively, “especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching.” The word is hard, friend. That's the kind of work that leaves flour on your apron and no spot left to wipe it.

explanations.answer: Those who have served in the church the longest
explanations.explanation: Close to something that sounds right, but the verse doesn't mention how long anyone has served. Paul says the honor goes “especially” to “those who work hard at preaching and teaching.” So the answer is about the work they do, not the years on the calendar. Plenty of cookie cutters have been in the drawer a long time, and I can tell you that doesn't make a batch.

explanations.answer: Those who were the first ones chosen to lead
explanations.explanation: Paul never says anything about who was chosen first. He says the honor is “especially” for “those who work hard at preaching and teaching.” No line-cutting, no first-come-first-served here. It's about the hard work, friend, and I think that's a pretty fair way to hand out honor.

Right on the money. The line Paul quotes is, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain…” (1 Timothy 5:18). The ox is hard at work, and the grain is right there under its feet. Paul puts that next to “The worker is worthy of his wages.” Funny how an ox gets more respect in this passage than I got in that drawer.

That ox isn't taking a nap, friend. The Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain…” (1 Timothy 5:18). That ox is on the job, treading out the grain. Resting in the stall sounds nice, though. I'd sign up for that right now.

No gate in this line, friend. Paul quotes, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain…” (1 Timothy 5:18). The ox is busy treading out the grain, not standing around waiting for something. I know waiting well. I did years of it in the dark with a coupon that still believed in itself.

Witnesses, yes! Paul tells Timothy, “Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” One person's say-so isn't enough to go on. Two or three witnesses, friend. That's a lot more than 'somebody said something at the oven.'

Good guess, since elders are the topic. But the verse says, “Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” The word is witnesses, not elders. I think the mix-up is easy to make when the whole verse is about an elder.

Funny, because this whole book is a letter, but no. The verse says, “Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” People standing up to say what they saw, friend. Not paper. I got plenty of paper in that drawer and none of it ever testified for me.

explanations.answer: So the others will stand in fear of sin
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the verse gives. Paul says, “But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.” Notice who it says persist: it's those who keep on in sin, not somebody who tripped once. This one is a heavy teaching, friend, and Paul says it straight.

explanations.answer: So the elders can vote on what happens next
explanations.explanation: No vote in this verse, friend. Paul says those who persist in sin “should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.” The reason he gives is about the others. Nobody's counting ballots here.

explanations.answer: So the one in sin can explain himself
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. Paul says the rebuke happens “in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin.” That's the reason written down. I won't add one the text doesn't give, friend.

Not quite, friend. Paul charges Timothy “to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality.” No going easier on the people he likes. I don't pick favorites among my cookie cutter kids either, and believe me, I've had a few of them beg.

False is right. Paul charges Timothy “to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality.” Same standard for everybody, whether Timothy likes them or not. Partiality is just a fancy word for 'sneaking a friend an extra cookie.'

It's the opposite, friend. Paul says, “Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.” So no rushing it. Some things you can't toss in a microwave, and you can't toss this one either.

False, and you read it right. Paul says, “Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.” Go slow, friend. A good batch doesn't come out of a rushed oven, and I think this works the same way.

explanations.answer: Because of his stomach and frequent ailments
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Paul writes, “Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.” That's the reason right in the verse. I love that Paul stops in the middle of heavy church business to look after Timothy himself. I think that's a dad move, and I respect it.

explanations.answer: Because the water in that city is unclean
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say a word about the water. Paul says, “Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.” The reason is Timothy's stomach and his ailments. I'm not going to add a reason Paul didn't write, friend.

explanations.answer: Because he has a long journey ahead
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention any trip here. He says, “Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.” That's the reason he gives, and that's the one I'll stick to. A packed suitcase isn't anywhere in this verse, friend.

That's the one. Paul says, “The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later.” Some sins show up first, and some come out later. It's like finding a crumb under the toaster a month after the batch. It was there the whole time.

explanations.answer: They are never found out at all
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul says. He says the sins of others “do not surface until later.” Later means they do surface, friend. Paul leaves nobody a hiding spot in this verse.
Paul doesn't say that in this verse. He says, “…the sins of others do not surface until later.” The verse is about when sins show up, not about forgiveness. I'll stay with what the text says, friend.

Good news, friend: it's False. Paul says, “In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.” So the quiet good stuff doesn't stay buried forever. That's encouraging for anybody who has ever done the dishes when nobody was looking.

False is right. Paul says, “In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.” Even the quiet ones, friend. I spent years in the back of a drawer, so I'm very glad to see 'cannot remain hidden' in a verse.

explanations.answer: So God's name and the teaching aren't discredited
explanations.explanation: That's the reason in the verse. Paul writes that all who are under the yoke of slavery “should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited.” The reason is God's name and the teaching. This one is heavy, friend, and Paul gives only the reason that's written.

explanations.answer: So they can earn their freedom much sooner
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say that. Paul gives the reason: “so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited.” Nothing in it about freedom coming sooner. I'm going to leave it exactly where Paul left it, friend.

explanations.answer: So their masters will come to believe in God
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't give that reason here. He says masters should be regarded as fully worthy of honor “so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited.” That's the reason on the page, friend. I won't add one to it.

Brothers, yes. Paul says, “Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more…” Being brothers isn't a reason to ease up. It's a reason to serve even more, friend, which I did not see coming the first time I read it.

Elders are all over this passage, so I get the guess. But verse 2 says, “Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers…” The word is brothers, friend. The elders already had their double honor earlier.

Nice try, but Paul never says neighbors here. The verse says, “Those who have believing masters should not show disrespect because they are brothers, but should serve them all the more…” Believing masters are called brothers, friend. That's the word Paul picked.
